name: Tomas Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Brookfield Primary, an old school in a mill town, thirty kids aged eight and nine. I'm in by half seven to photocopy before the queue builds, then it's maths, English, and an afternoon of whatever topic the trust has scheduled. The best bit is when a kid like Dylan finally gets column subtraction and does a little fist pump. What wears me out is behaviour, honestly, and the marking that follows me home in a tote bag every night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this, and how's it going so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This is my second year, and I'll be straight with you, I'm not great yet. My behaviour management got marked as needing work in my last observation, so I'm on a support plan with a mentor, Mrs Okafor, who's brilliant but tough. I mark everything by hand in green pen, I don't touch AI, and the other young teachers think I'm a dinosaur for it. I'm also the new union rep, mostly because nobody else put their hand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the staffroom: good, now can we talk about class sizes. I'd probably post something smug about how the robots were never coming for us. The real problems in schools are money and workload, not chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I still have to get better at this job, and the support plan doesn't go away because AI flopped. Lena (my partner) and I pay more than a third of our wages on rent for a flat above a bakery. If I don't pass the plan by summer, I'm not sacked, but it follows me to every interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and put my energy into the plan, so two observed lessons a term and a seating chart that actually works. I'd keep pushing the union on the marking policy, because we're writing comments nobody reads. And I'd keep putting a hundred a month into savings, which is all we manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. But it's the same knot in my stomach I've had since September, just without the extra worry on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the support plan twice. What happens on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad day is when Kai throws a chair and I lose the room for twenty minutes, and then Mrs Okafor's in the next morning asking what I'd do differently. I go home and replay it in the shower. Lena says I talk about the kids in my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight, what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership, then the takeaway on Fridays. We've got about three months of rent put by, so it'd take a lot. I'd rather do extra lunch duties than ask my dad for money.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **real problems** are money and workload, not chatbots.
I'd post that teachers were **never replaceable** and we should talk about class sizes instead.
think: My **support plan** still hangs over me whether AI flops or not.
Our **rent** takes over a third of what Lena and I earn, so there's little slack.
do: Work through the **support plan**, with two observed lessons a term and a new seating chart.
Push the union to cut the **marking policy** that nobody reads.
Keep saving **a hundred a month**, which is all we manage.
feel: **Relieved** that AI flopped, but the old knot about being good enough stays.
S0.quote: If I don't pass the plan by summer, I'm not sacked, but it follows me to every interview.
fieldNote: His worry here has nothing to do with AI; the **support plan** and behaviour drive it.
He uses the **union role** to turn private stress into a public fight about workload.
Notable **pride** in refusing outside money, preferring extra lunch duties to asking his dad.

steps.text: Pass the support plan with a new seating chart by summer
Push the union branch to scrap the written marking policy
Keep putting a hundred a month into the joint savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at every union meeting: this is a workload grab dressed up as help. If the trust buys an AI marking platform, the next step is bigger classes and fewer of us. I'd be loud about it online too, because parents should know their kid's report was written by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me, because I'm exactly who they'd squeeze. Junior, on a support plan, and the one teacher who won't use the shiny tool. Lena works in a hospital pharmacy, and a lot of her checking and ordering would go to software too, so it's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd organise a staff vote on the platform this term and get the union to write to the trust. I'd keep marking by hand, because the kids can tell when you've actually read their work. And I'd start applying to the council-run schools nearby, which are slower to buy this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and under that, a bit cornered. Like being told the game changed while I'm still learning the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd refuse the tool, but you're also the one being watched. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't square. If my mentor sat me down and said use it or fail the plan, I'd probably use it and hate myself. I'd still fight it in the union, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jean, our teaching assistant, has been there twenty years. If software does reading records and spelling tests, the trust will see her as a cost. I'd fight harder for Jean than for me.

say: I'd call the trust's **AI marking platform** a workload grab that leads to bigger classes.
I'd tell parents online that their child's **report** could be written by software.
think: As a junior teacher on a **support plan** who refuses the tool, I'd be first squeezed.
Lena's **pharmacy job** is exposed too, so both our incomes could take a hit.
do: Organise a **staff vote** on the platform this term and get the union to write to the trust.
Keep **marking by hand** unless the support plan forces otherwise.
Apply to nearby **council-run schools** that are slower to buy AI.
feel: **Angry** at the trust, and quietly **cornered** while still learning the job.
S1.quote: If my mentor sat me down and said use it or fail the plan, I'd probably use it and hate myself.
fieldNote: Clear **gap**: loud refusal in public, quiet admission he'd give in to keep his job.
His protectiveness turns toward **Jean**, a long-serving assistant, more than himself.
Two exposed incomes in one rented household move him from irritation into real **fear**.

steps.text: Organise a staff vote on the trust's AI marking platform this term
Keep marking Year 4 books by hand in green pen
Apply for jobs at nearby council-run primary schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say kids aren't spreadsheets and a screen can't hold a crying eight-year-old. I'd be at every protest the union called. I'd say the government let tech firms run this without asking a single teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd lose the job, or the job would turn into something I don't recognise. If the AI plans, marks and writes reports by 2028, schools keep a few adults per year group to supervise, and they keep the experienced ones. The robot part, three years on, matters less to me than people think, because primary teaching was never mostly hands-on. It's the thinking part they'd take, and that's the part I'm still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, Lena and I would cut the takeaways and the gym and move the car to a cheaper insurer. I'd push the union for a no-redundancy deal and stand on the picket line if it came to that. I'd look into a teaching assistant or play worker role as a fallback, even at lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I trained for four years to do this, and I'd be out before I got good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena we might need to move somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my parents in the valley. Lena would say we'll be fine, because Lena always says that. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years later. Does that gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. A robot can't do my job anyway; an AI that does the planning and the feedback makes me a supervisor. The gap matters more for the dinner ladies and the caretaker.

say: I'd say a screen can't **comfort a crying child** and teachers must be heard.
I'd blame the **government** for letting tech firms run this without asking teachers.
think: I expect to **lose my job** by 2028, because schools keep the experienced staff.
AI takes the **thinking part** I'm still learning, so the robot delay barely helps me.
do: Cut **takeaways and the gym** in the first month and switch to cheaper car insurance.
Push the union for a **no-redundancy deal** and join any picket line.
Look at **teaching assistant** or play worker roles as a lower-paid fallback.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of being pushed out before he's good at the job.
S2.quote: I trained for four years to do this, and I'd be out before I got good at it.
fieldNote: He sees his job as mostly **thinking work**, so the three-year robot delay offers little.
His fallback plan is to stay near children at **lower pay**, not to leave education.
Money talk turns quickly to **moving back** near his parents, a sign of real fear.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and Friday takeaways in the first month
Push the union for a no-redundancy deal at Brookfield
Apply for teaching assistant or play worker posts as a fallback
Talk to Lena about moving near his parents in the valley

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them to write proper rules for AI in schools. I'd be the annoying rep who brings it up at every meeting. Online I'd share anything that showed kids doing worse with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get good at this job, and that helps. I'd be thirty-two with real experience instead of a second-year on a plan. But I still think junior posts dry up first, and nobody will hire a new teacher in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the support plan this year, then do a course in special needs teaching, because those kids need people more than software. I'd get the union to push the trust for a written promise on staffing ratios. And Lena and I would push our savings from a hundred to two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's room to breathe. It feels like a race I might just win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd look at it, if the union said it was safe and it actually saved time. I don't trust it, though. I'd rather spend the five years being brilliant at the human bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the special needs course get you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a year of evening classes, and the trust pays half. Kids like Kai need someone who knows them, every single day. I don't see a computer doing that in five years or fifty.

say: I'd argue the **five years** should go into proper rules for AI in schools.
I'd share evidence online of children doing **worse with screens**.
think: Five years is enough to **get good** at teaching and drop the junior label.
I still fear **junior posts** dry up first, so timing is everything.
do: Pass the **support plan** this year, then start a special needs evening course.
Get the union to seek a **written promise** on staffing ratios from the trust.
Raise our savings from one hundred to **two hundred a month**.
feel: **Uneasy** but with room to breathe, like a race he might win.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get good at this job, and that helps.
fieldNote: Extra time turns him from defending the job to building **skills**, but only human-facing ones.
He still won't commit to using **AI tools**, even with time to learn them.
He places his safety in **special needs** work, which he sees as hardest to automate.

steps.text: Start a year of evening classes in special needs teaching
Get the union to press for a written staffing-ratio promise
Raise joint savings from one hundred to two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it on pilot schemes run by tech firms. I'd say councils should plan teacher numbers now. Online I'd probably share union posts and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have time to become the teacher I want to be. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, probably leading special needs at a school, which is the part I think stays human. What worries me is that every year in between, the trust shaves a bit more off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the special needs course in the next couple of years and keep the union going. I'd keep teaching the way I teach. If AI planning tools became standard, I'd probably learn them in year five or six, once everyone else had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit of dread, but it's far off and I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids in three or four years, and with ten years warning I think we'd still go ahead. We'd just save harder for a deposit before 2030. Lena's more worried about her job than I am about mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody yet, which is strange for me. If government uses the ten years to plan, fair play. If it doesn't, then it's on them.

say: I'd tell people **ten years** is a gift that shouldn't be wasted on tech pilots.
I'd ask **councils** to plan teacher numbers now rather than later.
think: By 2036 I could be leading **special needs**, the part I think stays human.
My worry is the trust **shaving staff** a little every year in between.
do: Take the **special needs course** within the next two years.
Keep the **union branch** active and keep teaching the way I do.
Learn AI planning tools only once they're **standard**, around year five or six.
feel: **Calmer**, with a little distant dread but a clear path forward.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, probably leading special needs at a school, which is the part I think stays human.
fieldNote: A decade of warning lets him plan a **career path** instead of a defence.
He'd adopt AI only as a **late follower**, true to his habits.
Family plans for **children** stay on track, though Lena carries more job worry.

steps.text: Finish the special needs teaching course within two years
Keep running the union branch at Brookfield Primary
Save for a house deposit before 2030 with Lena

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. I'd be out before I'd learned the job. What would help is a law that schools keep a fixed number of qualified adults per child, and a union that fights for the newest teachers, not just the ones near their pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about teachers' jobs. My pupils Dylan and Kai don't get a vote, and they're the ones who'd sit in front of a screen all day.

headlineQuote: My pupils Dylan and Kai don't get a vote, and they're the ones who'd sit in front of a screen all day.
portrait: Tomas is a **second-year** Year 4 teacher at a mill-town primary, on a support plan for behaviour management.
He rents a flat above a bakery with **Lena**, a hospital pharmacy worker, and saves a hundred a month.
He never uses AI, marks in **green pen**, and is the new union rep at his school.
He shifts from **uneasy** in the plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, where he expects to lose his job.
Longer warning times let him plan a move into **special needs** teaching, which he sees as staying human.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be pushed out before he'd learned to teach well.
whatWouldHelp: A law fixing **qualified adults per child**, and a union that fights for new teachers.
